title: Zero-Energy Building Rules
inOneSentence: Korea's national rules grade new buildings by how much of their own energy they make, and the rules started with public buildings in 2020 and reached private buildings in 2025.
background: Korea has a national system for zero-energy buildings, called ZEB for short. It is run by MOLIT, the national Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport. Seoul's climate plan builds on this national system. So the rules on this slide apply across all of Korea, and Seoul's plan adds its own targets for new public buildings.

The system grades a building by its energy self-sufficiency rate. That is the share of the energy a building uses that it also makes itself, mostly with renewable systems such as solar panels. There are five grades. Grade 5 is the entry level, at 20 to 40%. Grade 1 is the top, at over 100%, which means the building makes more energy than it uses over a year. Your sources don't give confirmed percentages for Grades 4, 3 and 2. You only need to know that they sit between the two ends.

The rules came in steps, starting with the government's own buildings. In 2020, new public buildings over 1,000 m² had to meet ZEB status, and the size limit was later lowered to 500 m². In 2023, the public sector moved to Grade 5. The rule for private buildings was planned for 2024. It was pushed back one year after the construction industry objected, and talks with the industry ran into mid-2025. From 2025, private apartment complexes of 30 or more units and buildings over 1,000 m² in general have to meet Grade 5. Some sources also report a goal of making all new buildings in Korea zero-energy by 2030, but that date is less certain. Sources give slightly different dates for these steps, and you should say so on stage.
Seoul's climate plan sets its own targets for new public buildings: Grade 5 now, Grade 4 by 2030 and Grade 3 by 2050. So the plan raises the grade for new public buildings step by step over time.

This slide matters for the talk because it shows where the firm rules are. They come from Korea's national ZEB system, which Seoul's plan builds on, and they apply when a new building is designed and built. For buildings that already exist, Seoul leans on cheap loans (slide 8). New York's Local Law 97 covers large buildings over 25,000 sq ft, and most of those buildings already exist. It sets yearly carbon limits per square foot and fines owners who go over. The quote from MOLIT's Hong Seongjun explains why the private rule matters. Most buildings are private, so a rule for public buildings alone would reach only the smaller share of buildings.

explainSimply: Think of it as a report card for how much of its own power a building makes. A Grade 5 building makes about a fifth to two fifths of the energy it uses, mostly from solar panels. A Grade 1 building makes more than it uses over a year. Korea started by asking for Grade 5, first from government buildings and then from private ones, and Seoul's plan raises the grade for new public buildings over time.

questions.q: What does "energy self-sufficiency" actually mean?
questions.a: It's the share of the energy a building uses that it also makes itself, mostly from things like solar panels. If a building uses 100 units of energy in a year and its own systems make 30, its self-sufficiency is 30%, which puts it in Grade 5.

questions.q: Why did Korea start with public buildings?
questions.a: One likely reason is that the government controls its own buildings, so it can test the rules there first. My sources give the order, with public buildings from 2020 and private buildings from 2025, but they don't state the reason. The next slides show two of Seoul's own public buildings, City Hall and the Energy Dream Center.

questions.q: Grade 5 only needs 20 to 40%. Can you really call that a zero-energy building?
questions.a: That's a fair point. A Grade 5 building still gets most of its energy from the grid, and only Grade 1 makes all of its own. The name covers the whole ladder, and Grade 5 is the first step. Seoul's plan moves new public buildings up to Grade 4 by 2030 and Grade 3 by 2050.

questions.q: Why was the private rule delayed, and what exactly do private apartments have to reach?
questions.a: It was planned for 2024 and delayed one year after the construction industry pushed back, with talks running into mid-2025. On the exact requirement my sources disagree. One says new private apartments must make at least 13% of their own energy, and another says 40% for complexes of 30 or more units, so I don't give one number.

questions.q: How does this compare with New York's rules?
questions.a: They mostly reach different buildings and they measure different things. Korea's ZEB rules apply to new buildings and grade how much energy they make for themselves. New York's Local Law 97 applies to large buildings over 25,000 sq ft, most of which are already built. It limits how much carbon they emit per square foot each year and fines owners $268 for every ton over the limit.

Don't give one figure for what private apartments must reach. Sources say 13% or 40%, and they seem to be different measures.
Don't present 2030 as a fixed deadline for all new buildings. It is reported in some sources and less certain.
Don't treat the rollout dates as exact. Sources give slightly different dates, so say that out loud.
Don't call the ZEB system a Seoul law. It is national and run by MOLIT. Seoul's plan builds on it.
Don't say every zero-energy building makes all of its own energy. Only Grade 1 does. Grade 5 makes 20 to 40%.
Don't give the Energy Dream Center a ZEB grade or call it Grade 1. No source gives it one.

nycLink: This slide shows where the stick is in Seoul's approach. The firm rules come from Korea's national ZEB system, which Seoul's plan builds on, and they apply to new buildings. For existing buildings Seoul uses cheap loans (slide 8). New York's main tool, Local Law 97, sets limits and fines for large buildings over 25,000 sq ft, and most of those buildings already exist. The two systems also measure different things. Korea grades how much energy a building makes for itself, and LL97 limits how much carbon a building emits per square foot each year. The photo pair after this slide shows a public building from each city, since Korea's rules started with public buildings.

title: Public Buildings Go First
seoul: Seoul City Hall, opened in 2012 and designed by iArc Architects (Yoo Keri won the design competition). A wave of glass curves over the preserved 1926 colonial-era city hall, and inside there is a green wall of 1,516 m² that runs from floor 1 to floor 7. The city says about 28% of the building's energy comes from solar panels, solar heating and geothermal (28.3% is the city's own figure; Wikipedia says over 25%). Many critics disliked the glass wave next to the old building.
nyc: P.S. 62, The Kathleen Grimm School for Leadership and Sustainability, a public school on Staten Island. The photo plan describes it as New York's first net-zero energy school. Your dossier doesn't cover this school, so check that claim before you say it out loud, or just call it a public school built around sustainability.
why: Both are government buildings that show green design to the public. Korea's zero-energy rules started with public buildings in 2020, so this pair puts a public building from each city side by side.

title: Seoul Energy Dream Center
inOneSentence: The Energy Dream Center, opened in 2012 on the old Nanjido landfill, is Korea's first zero-energy public building and covers its own yearly energy use.
background: The Seoul Energy Dream Center opened in 2012 in World Cup Park, in the Mapo-gu district. It is Korea's first zero-energy public building. It is about 3,500 m² and works as a public exhibition and education center about renewable energy. The Seoul city government commissioned it. The design was led by Fraunhofer ISE, a German research institute for solar energy, which ran a German and Korean team that designed the building and oversaw construction.

The site is the old Nanjido landfill from slide 4. Nanjido was an island in the Han River that became Seoul's official dump in 1978. Trash piled up about 90 m high in two mounds, and there was no modern system to treat the gas or the polluted liquid coming out of it. The city decided to close the dump in 1993, and the site reopened as World Cup Park for the 2002 World Cup. Landfill gas is now captured and used. Trash can't carry the weight of a building, so the Energy Dream Center stands on piles that go down through the waste to solid ground, with a reinforced concrete base plate on top.

The shape is the first energy strategy. The plan is square. The building widens as it rises over its three floors and turns 45°, with a square roof on top. From outside it looks a bit like a pinwheel with slanted walls, and it was shaped this way to cut how much energy the building needs. Wedge-shaped roof edges, called wings, stick out along the sides. They shade the windows, give cover at the entrance and hold solar panels. The white marble outside walls reflect sunlight, and one source says they reflect about 60% of it.

The envelope, meaning the walls, roof and windows, was designed to Passive House standards, so it is very well insulated and airtight. Geothermal heat pumps handle heating and cooling. Solar panels on the roof, on the wings and on a small patch of ground supply about 280,000 kWh a year, which covers the building's full yearly demand. The building stays connected to the power grid. It can send extra power out on sunny days and draw power when the panels make less than it needs. It is reported to use over 70% less energy than a similar ordinary building, and it holds Korea's KGBC green building certification and the Building Energy Efficiency Label.

The building connects the landfill story and the zero-energy story. It sits on the landfill Seoul turned into a park, and it shows the zero-energy idea from slide 9 working on a real public building in 2012, years before the national rule for public buildings began in 2020. New York has its own landfill that is becoming a park, Freshkills Park on Staten Island, so this is a place where the two cities line up closely.

explainSimply: Think of the building as having an energy savings account. On sunny days its solar panels make more power than it needs and send the extra to the grid. At night and on cloudy days it takes power back from the grid. Over a full year the two even out. And because it stands on old trash, it rests on long concrete legs that go down through the garbage to firm ground, the way a table could stand on long legs that reach through a pile of loose sand.
sayThis: Remember Nanjido from earlier? This building sits right on top of it.

questions.q: How do you put a building on top of a landfill?
questions.a: Trash is too loose and soft to hold up a building, so the Energy Dream Center sits on piles. These are long columns that go down through the waste to solid ground, and a reinforced concrete base plate on top spreads the building's weight onto them. Landfill gas at World Cup Park is also captured and used.

questions.q: If it makes all its own energy, why is it still connected to the grid?
questions.a: Zero energy here means over a whole year. On sunny days the panels make more than the building needs and the extra goes to the grid, and at night or on dark days it draws power back. Over the year its panels make about as much as it uses, around 280,000 kWh.

questions.q: Who was the architect?
questions.a: The design was led by Fraunhofer ISE, Germany's Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems, with a German and Korean team working for the Seoul city government. Some websites credit Gerkan Marg & Partners, but I couldn't confirm that, so I credit Fraunhofer ISE as the design lead.

questions.q: It's a small exhibition building that nobody lives in. Isn't that the easy case?
questions.a: Yes, it's an easier case than housing. It's a fairly small public building of about 3,500 m², built as a showcase. That's why the next slide looks at the Nowon apartments, which aim for net zero and are reported to make about 75 to 80% of their own energy.

questions.q: Over 70% less energy than what?
questions.a: Than a similar ordinary building, as reported in my sources. They don't describe the comparison building in detail, so I present it as a reported figure. The solar output of about 280,000 kWh a year is the firmer number.

Don't say the building is off the grid or makes all its own power every hour. Its panels cover its yearly demand, and it stays connected to the grid.
Don't give it a ZEB grade or call it Grade 1. No source gives it one.
Don't call it a certified Passive House. Say its envelope was built to Passive House standards. The first Korean housing with German Passive House certification is Building 102 at Nowon (slide 11).
Don't present the 70% saving as a measured result. It is a reported figure.
Don't state the 60% marble reflection as a firm fact. Only one source gives it.
Don't call it the world's first zero-energy building. It is Korea's first zero-energy public building.

terms.meaning: A building whose own renewable systems make as much energy over a full year as it uses. On some days it makes more and on others less, and the grid balances the difference.
The Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems, a German research institute. It led the German and Korean design team for the Energy Dream Center.

A German standard for buildings that are very well insulated and very airtight, so they need very little energy for heating and cooling.
The outer skin of a building: its walls, roof, windows and floor slab, which separate inside from outside.
A system that uses the steady temperature of the ground. Fluid runs through pipes buried in the ground to heat pumps, which pull heat out of the ground in winter and push heat into it in summer.

terms.meaning: Korea's Green Building Certification and its national energy efficiency rating for buildings. The Energy Dream Center holds both.

Seoul took one more step and put a zero-energy teaching building on its old landfill. This supports the talk's point that Seoul's government uses its own buildings to lead and to teach the public before it asks private owners to follow. The photo after this slide pairs the Energy Dream Center with the Queens Botanical Garden visitor center, another public building people visit to learn.

title: Buildings That Teach
seoul: The Seoul Energy Dream Center from outside, in World Cup Park on the old Nanjido landfill. In the photo, look for the floors getting wider as they rise and the wing-like roof edges that shade the windows and hold solar panels. Its panels cover its full yearly demand of about 280,000 kWh.
nyc: The Queens Botanical Garden Visitor and Administration Center in Flushing, Queens, a public building where visitors come to learn about plants and nature. Your dossier has no figures for this building, so describe what the photo shows and leave out ratings or energy numbers.
why: Both are public buildings that people visit to learn. The Energy Dream Center is an exhibition and education center about energy, and the building itself is a working example of what it shows.

title: Nowon Energy Zero House
inOneSentence: Nowon Energy Zero House, finished in 2017 with 121 homes in Nowon-gu, is Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex, and it raises the question of what New York could build for its own apartments under Local Law 97.
background: Nowon Energy Zero House, often called EZ House, is in Nowon-gu, a district of Seoul. It is Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex, with 121 apartments. It was finished in September 2017, and residents moved in from November 2017. Of all the Seoul buildings in the talk, this one matters most for New York, because New York has a huge number of apartment buildings and apartments are much harder to get to zero energy than a showcase building like the Energy Dream Center.

The goal is net zero over a year, counted in primary energy. That means the complex aims to make as much energy as it uses over a full year. The reported result is that it makes about 75 to 80% of its own energy, so say it aims for net zero and makes most of its own energy. Residents' energy costs are reported to be up to 61% lower than in similar ordinary apartments.

The dossier sums up the design as a passive envelope plus renewables. These are known building parts used together. From the bottom up, the diagram shows a geothermal field with about 130 heat pumps, the structure, a Passive House envelope, heat recovery ventilation and, last, the solar panels. A Passive House envelope generally means thick insulation, an airtight layer and very good windows. Heat recovery ventilation brings in fresh air all the time and uses the stale air going out to warm or cool it, so little heat is lost. Heat recovery is shown on the diagram, but the dossier lists only a passive envelope plus renewables, so describe it in general terms if asked. Sources count the solar panels differently, 1,284 in one and 1,800 in another, so say about 1,300 to 1,800 panels.

It was built through a national research program run by MOLIT, working with the city of Seoul and the Nowon-gu district, with companies and universities as partners. So the national government, the city and the district all had a role. In August 2018, Building 102 became the first housing in Korea to earn German Passive House certification. In December 2017, President Moon Jae-in visited, called it Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex, and used it to start a national push to build more like it.

The New York link is Local Law 97. For large apartment buildings over 25,000 sq ft, the yearly carbon limit drops by about half in 2030. The exact figures are 0.00675 t CO₂e per sq ft a year for 2024 to 2029 and about 0.00335 (0.003346640) for 2030 to 2034, a 50.4% cut. About 63% of the buildings LL97 covers are projected to go over their 2030 limits if nothing changes. Your question to the room asks what a NYCHA version of Nowon would look like. To answer it, the class has to think about who pays and who builds, along with the design.

questions.q: Does it actually reach net zero?
questions.a: It aims for net zero over a year. The reported figure is that it makes about 75 to 80% of its own energy, so I say it aims for net zero and makes most of its own energy. Residents' energy costs are reported to be up to 61% lower than in similar ordinary apartments.

questions.q: How much did it cost to build?
questions.a: The published figures don't agree. Different sources give about US$4.5 million, US$18 million and US$49 million, so I don't use any of them.

questions.q: What makes it zero-energy?
questions.a: It aims for net zero, and it gets most of the way there with several known parts working together. A very well insulated, airtight Passive House envelope cuts how much heating and cooling the apartments need, and heat recovery ventilation keeps fresh air coming in without losing much heat. Then the geothermal heat pumps and about 1,300 to 1,800 solar panels supply most of the small amount of energy that is left.

questions.q: Does NYCHA actually have to meet the LL97 limit you showed?
questions.a: My sources don't say which LL97 limits apply to NYCHA buildings, so I'm not claiming that. What I can say is that the limit for large apartment buildings over 25,000 sq ft drops by about half in 2030. That's why I framed it as a question.

questions.q: Could New York really build something like this? Who would pay for it?
questions.a: Nowon was developed through a national research program run by MOLIT with the city of Seoul and the Nowon-gu district, plus companies and universities. New York would likely need a similar partnership to share the cost and risk of a first project. That's why my NYCHA question points at who pays and who builds, along with the design.

title: Zero-Energy Housing
seoul: Nowon Energy Zero House in Nowon-gu, Seoul, Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex. It has 121 apartments, and in August 2018 its Building 102 became the first housing in Korea to earn German Passive House certification.
nyc: Sendero Verde in East Harlem, a large new housing complex. The photo plan describes it as large Passive House housing. Your dossier has no figures for it, so don't give unit counts or energy numbers.
why: Both are new apartment complexes designed to use very little energy. Nowon is the Seoul building that matters most for New York, because so much of New York's housing is in apartment buildings.

title: Two LEED Gold Buildings
inOneSentence: Amorepacific HQ and Lotte World Tower, two large Seoul buildings finished in 2017, both earned LEED Gold, but Amorepacific's green design comes mostly from its shape while Lotte relies mostly on added equipment, which raises the question of what LEED really measures.
background: LEED is a green building rating from the US Green Building Council. It has four levels, Certified, Silver, Gold and Platinum, so Gold is the second highest. Both buildings on this slide were finished in 2017 and both are LEED Gold, which makes them a good pair to compare.

Amorepacific HQ was designed by David Chipperfield Architects, with Arup as the engineers for the building systems. The design won a competition in 2010, construction started in 2014 and the building was finished in 2017. The company has been on this site since 1956. The building is a large cube around a central courtyard, with its proportions worked out so that natural air flow and daylight work well. Three large openings, called hanging gardens, cut through the outside walls and connect the courtyard to the outside, bringing light and air deep inside. Fins on the facade cut sun and glare. It got LEED Gold in 2018 under Core & Shell, which rates the base building only. It has about 22 floors above ground and roughly 7,000 to 8,000 people working there.

Lotte World Tower was designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox (KPF). It is 555 m tall with 123 floors, one of the tallest buildings in the world, and its form draws on Korean ceramics, porcelain and calligraphy. It relies mostly on added systems. It has 720 geothermal wells about 200 m deep, uses Han River water for heating and cooling, and has wind turbines near the top, solar panels and energy recovery wheels that pass heat from outgoing air to incoming air. It also reuses greywater and collects rainwater. One source reports it as the first building over 100 floors to earn LEED Gold.

Amorepacific also won a CIBSE Building Performance Award. CIBSE is the UK professional body for the engineers who design heating, cooling and lighting, and this award is judged on measured performance, meaning real data from the building in use. So Amorepacific has evidence that it works in practice, in addition to its LEED rating.

The main point of the slide is what LEED measures. LEED Gold shows that a building is efficient for its type. The dossier says LEED Gold on Lotte certifies relative efficiency. For the energy score, LEED compares the design with a standard version of the same building that just meets a basic energy code (general knowledge). So "a normal tower like it" in your quote means that standard version of Lotte. If someone asks which towers, explain that it is a model of the same building. A 555 m tower still has a huge amount of embodied carbon, which is the carbon released to make all that concrete and steel and to build with it, and it uses a lot of energy for each person inside. So the same LEED Gold rating covers two buildings that reach it in very different ways.

explainSimply: LEED's energy score works a bit like rating a car's fuel use against a standard car of the same size. A big SUV can score well for an SUV and still burn far more fuel than a small car. Lotte scores well for a supertall, and it is still a 555 m tower full of concrete and steel. Amorepacific is more like a car that was tested on the road, because its CIBSE award was based on real measured data.
sayThis: LEED's energy score compares Lotte to a normal tower like it.

questions.q: What does LEED Gold mean?
questions.a: LEED is the US Green Building Council's green building rating. It has four levels, Certified, Silver, Gold and Platinum, so Gold is the second highest. Buildings earn points for things like energy, water and materials, and the total sets the level.

questions.q: What does Core & Shell mean?
questions.a: It's a LEED rating for the base building: the structure, the outside walls and the central systems like heating and cooling. It leaves out the tenants' interiors. Amorepacific got LEED Gold under Core & Shell in 2018.

questions.q: Why does the CIBSE award matter?
questions.a: CIBSE is the UK professional body for building services engineers, the people who design heating, cooling and lighting. Its Building Performance Award is judged on measured performance, using data from the building in use. So it shows Amorepacific performs well in real life, which adds something a design rating on its own can't show.

questions.q: So which building does more for the climate: Lotte, Amorepacific or Nowon?
questions.a: LEED can't settle that, because its energy score compares each building with a standard version of its own type. Amorepacific has measured data behind its award, and Nowon is a 121-unit apartment complex that aims for net zero. Lotte is efficient for a supertall, but a 555 m tower carries huge embodied carbon and high energy use per person, so I find it hard to argue it does the most for the climate.

questions.q: Lotte has geothermal wells, river water heating and cooling, wind turbines and solar panels. Why criticize it?
questions.a: The equipment helps, but the size of the tower is the bigger issue. Building 555 m and 123 floors takes an enormous amount of concrete and steel, and the carbon from making those materials is released before anyone moves in. LEED Gold shows Lotte is efficient for its type, so it doesn't answer the question of total carbon.

dontSay: Don't say Lotte has solar panels built into its facade as a fact. Say "solar panels, and one source says some are built into the facade."

Don't say Lotte was definitely the first building over 100 floors with LEED Gold. Say one source reports it.
Don't give 216,000 m² or 30 floors for Amorepacific. Sources conflict, so use about 22 floors above ground.
Don't say LEED Gold means a building is low carbon. The rating shows a building is efficient for its type, and its energy score compares the building with a standard version of itself.
Don't call Gold the top LEED level. Platinum is higher.
Don't say Amorepacific's interiors were rated. Core & Shell covers the base building only.
Don't give a number for Lotte's embodied carbon. The dossier has none.
If you mention that Amorepacific is a Korean cosmetics company, know that it comes from general knowledge. The dossier doesn't say it.

nycLink: New York is full of tall towers. One World Trade Center, in the photo after this slide, raises the same question as Lotte. Local Law 97 works in another way. It caps each large building's carbon per square foot every year. That carbon is worked out from the energy each building reports using that year (general knowledge), which is closer to the CIBSE measured approach than to a design rating. For the talk, this slide shows that Seoul's showcase towers deserve the same honest look as New York's, and it sets up the question of what cities should reward.

title: Two Supertalls
seoul: Lotte World Tower, 555 m tall with 123 floors, designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox and finished in 2017. It is LEED Gold and uses 720 geothermal wells and Han River water for heating and cooling.
nyc: One World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan, one of the tallest buildings in New York (general knowledge). Your dossier has no figures for it, so don't quote its height or any rating from memory.
why: Both are supertall towers that stand out in their city's skyline. The embodied carbon point from slide 12 applies to both, since a very tall tower takes a huge amount of concrete and steel whatever rating it earns.
